blocks.text: K. stared at the Inspector. Was he to receive schoolmasterly lessons here from a man who was perhaps younger than himself? Was he to be punished for his candor with a rebuke? And was he to learn nothing about the reason for his arrest and about those who had ordered it?

He fell into a certain agitation, walked up and down, which nobody prevented him from doing, pushed back his cuffs, felt his chest, smoothed his hair into place, passed by the three gentlemen, said, "It makes no sense at all," whereupon they turned toward him and looked at him obligingly, yet seriously, and finally came to a halt again before the Inspector's table. "Public Prosecutor Hasterer is a good friend of mine," he said, "may I telephone him?" "Certainly," said the Inspector, "but I do not know what sense there would be in that, unless you have some private matter of your own to discuss with him." "What sense?" cried K., more dismayed than annoyed. "Who are you, anyway? You demand sense and you are staging the most senseless thing there is. Is it not enough to make a stone weep? These gentlemen first ambushed me and now they sit or stand around here and make me go through my paces before you. What sense there would be in telephoning a public prosecutor when I am supposedly under arrest? Very well, I shall not telephone." "By all means do," said the Inspector, stretching out his hand toward the anteroom where the telephone was, "please, do telephone." "No, I no longer wish to," said K. and went to the window. Over across the way the party was still at the window, and only now, because K. had stepped up to the window, did the quiet of their watching seem a little disturbed. The old people wanted to rise, but the man behind them calmed them down. "There are onlookers of the same sort over there too," K. called out quite loudly to the Inspector, pointing outside with his forefinger. "Away from there," he then called across. The three did immediately retreat a few steps, the two old people even withdrawing behind the man, who shielded them with his broad body and, to judge from the movements of his mouth, was saying something unintelligible at that distance. Yet they did not vanish entirely, but seemed to be waiting for the moment when they could approach the window again unnoticed. "Intrusive, inconsiderate people!" said K. as he turned back into the room. The Inspector possibly agreed with him, as K. thought he could tell with a sidelong glance. But it was just as possible that he had not been listening at all, for he had pressed one hand firmly flat upon the table and seemed to be comparing the fingers according to their length. The two warders sat on a trunk draped with an ornamental cover and rubbed their knees. The three young men had set their hands on their hips and were looking aimlessly around. It was as quiet as in some forgotten office. "Now then, gentlemen," cried K.—for a moment it seemed to him as though he were carrying them all on his shoulders—"to judge by your appearance, my affair would seem to be concluded. I am of the opinion that it is best to think no more about the justification or lack of justification for your conduct and to bring the matter to a conciliatory close with a mutual handshake. If you too are of my opinion, then please"—and he stepped up to the Inspector's table and held out his hand to him. The Inspector raised his eyes, bit his lips, and looked at K.'s outstretched hand; K. still believed the Inspector would take it. The latter, however, stood up, picked up a hard round hat that was lying on Fräulein Bürstner's bed, and put it on carefully with both hands, as one does when trying on new hats. "How simple everything seems to you!" he said to K. as he did so, "we should bring the matter to a conciliatory close, you thought? No, no, that really will not do. By which, on the other hand, I by no means wish to say that you ought to despair. No, why should you? You are merely under arrest, nothing more. That was what I had to communicate to you, I have done so, and I have also seen how you took it. With that it is enough for today and we can take our leave, though only for the time being. You will doubtless want to go to the Bank now?" "To the Bank?" asked K., "I thought I was under arrest." K. asked with a certain defiance, for although his handshake had not been accepted, he felt himself, particularly since the Inspector had stood up, increasingly independent of all these people. He was playing with them. He had the intention, in case they should leave, of running after them as far as the house gate and offering them his arrest. That was why he also repeated: "How can I go to the Bank, since I am under arrest?" "Ah, I see," said the Inspector, who was already at the door, "you have misunderstood me. You are under arrest, certainly, but that need not hinder you from carrying out your profession. Nor are you to be hindered in your ordinary course of life." "Then being under arrest is not very bad," said K., walking up close to the Inspector. "I never meant it otherwise," said the latter. "In that case, however, even the notification of the arrest does not seem to have been very necessary," said K., coming closer still. The others had drawn near as well. All of them were now gathered in a narrow space by the door. "It was my duty," said the Inspector. "A stupid duty," said K. unyieldingly. "That may be," replied the Inspector, "but we do not want to waste our time with such talk. I had assumed that you would want to go to the Bank. Since you pay heed to every word, I will add: I am not forcing you to go to the Bank, I had merely assumed that you wanted to. And in order to make that easier for you, and to render your arrival at the Bank as inconspicuous as possible, I have kept these three gentlemen, your colleagues, here at your disposal." "What?" cried K., staring at the three in astonishment. These so uncharacteristic, anemic young men, whom he still remembered only as a group beside the photographs, were actually clerks from his Bank—not colleagues, that was saying too much and already betrayed a gap in the Inspector's omniscience, but subordinate clerks from the Bank they certainly were. How could K. have overlooked that? How absorbed he must have been by the Inspector and the warders not to recognize these three! Stiff Rabensteiner, swinging his hands, blond Kullich with the deep-set eyes, and Kaminer with his insufferable smile caused by a chronic muscular twitch—"Good morning!" said K. after a brief moment, extending his hand to the gentlemen, who bowed correctly. "I did not recognize you at all. Well then, we shall go to work now, shall we not?" The gentlemen nodded eagerly and laughingly, as though they had been waiting for that the whole time; only when K. missed his hat, which had been left behind in his room, did they all run one after another to fetch it, which after all pointed to a certain embarrassment. K. stood still and watched them through the two open doors; the last, of course, was the indifferent Rabensteiner, who had broken into no more than an elegant trot. Kaminer handed over the hat and K. had to tell himself expressly, as indeed was often necessary in the Bank as well, that Kaminer's smile was not deliberate, in fact that he could not smile deliberately at all. In the anteroom Frau Grubach, who did not look particularly guilty at all, then opened the front door of the flat for the whole company, and K., as so often, looked down at her apron string, which cut so needlessly deep into her massive body. Downstairs, watch in hand, K. decided to take a motor-car so as not to prolong needlessly a delay that already amounted to half an hour. Kaminer ran to the corner to fetch the cab; the two others were obviously trying to distract K., when suddenly Kullich pointed to the house doorway opposite, in which the tall man with the blond pointed beard had just appeared and in the first moment, a little embarrassed at showing himself now in his full height, stepped back against the wall and leaned there. The old people were probably still on the stairs. K. was annoyed with Kullich for calling attention to the man whom he himself had already seen earlier, indeed whom he had even been expecting. "Do not look over there!" he blurted out, without noticing how striking such a way of speaking was toward independent men. However, no explanation was needed either, for the motor-car arrived just then, they took their seats and drove off. Then K. remembered that he had not noticed the departure of the Inspector and the warders at all; the Inspector had screened the three clerks from him, and now in turn the clerks had screened the Inspector. That did not show much presence of mind, and K. resolved to watch himself more closely in this respect. Nevertheless, he involuntarily turned around once more and leaned forward over the folded hood at the back of the motor-car in order possibly still to catch sight of the Inspector and the warders. But right away he turned back again and leaned comfortably into the corner of the cab without even having made the attempt to look for anyone. Even though it did not appear so, it was just now that he would have needed encouragement, yet now the gentlemen seemed tired; Rabensteiner looked out of the car to the right, Kullich to the left, and only Kaminer remained available with his grin, about which humanity unfortunately forbade making a joke.
